overview: Vision is organized as a largely hierarchical, retinotopic pathway from retina through the lateral geniculate nucleus to primary visual cortex, then diverges into two cortical streams: a dorsal 'where/how' stream (MT/V5 → posterior parietal) for spatial vision and visually guided action, and a ventral 'what' stream (V4 → inferior temporal) for object, face, and scene recognition. A parallel retinotectal route through the superior colliculus supports reflexive orienting and residual vision in blindsight.

citations.source: Kandel et al., Principles of Neural Science, 6th ed. (2021), Ch. 25–28
Purves et al., Principles of Cognitive Neuroscience, 2nd ed. (2013), Ch. 8

function: Thalamic relay of the retina to primary visual cortex; laminar organization segregates magnocellular, parvocellular, and koniocellular channels.
Receives strong corticofugal feedback and reticular modulation, gating visual throughput during arousal.

efferent: Primary visual cortex via the optic radiation

clinical.note: LGN or optic-radiation damage produces quadrantanopia or hemianopia respecting the vertical meridian.

function: Primary visual cortex (V1, Brodmann area 17); the first cortical stage, with a precise retinotopic map and orientation-selective columns.
Reconstructs edges and motion signals that are redistributed to extrastriate areas.

clinical.note: Bilateral V1 lesions cause blindness with preserved pupillary reflexes; unilateral lesions cause contralateral hemianopia.

function: Region containing area MT/V5, specialized for visual motion and heading; integrates motion signals for smooth pursuit and optic flow.
A hub of the dorsal 'where/how' stream.

clinical.note: Bilateral MT+ lesions cause selective motion blindness (e.g., patient L.M.).

function: High-level ventral-stream cortex for object, face, and visual-form recognition; cells show increasing invariance to position and scale.

clinical.note: Bilateral IT damage produces apperceptive/associative agnosia or prosopagnosia (face blindness).

function: Midbrain retinotopic map mediating reflexive saccades and orienting; part of the retinotectal pathway.
Believed to support residual visual function in blindsight following V1 damage.

clinical.note: Residual above-chance visual discrimination despite V1 lesions, attributed to the colliculo-pulvinar route.

questions.stem: Which two cortical streams were proposed by Ungerleider & Mishkin, and later reframed by Goodale & Milner?
questions.explanation: Ungerleider & Mishkin (1982) proposed dorsal 'where' and ventral 'what' streams; Goodale & Milner (1992) reframed the dorsal stream as 'how' (visually guided action).

questions.stem: Bilateral lesions of area MT/V5 classically produce which selective deficit?
questions.explanation: Patient L.M. (Zihl et al., 1983) could not perceive motion after bilateral MT+ damage, a syndrome termed akinetopsia.

questions.stem: The koniocellular, parvocellular, and magnocellular channels of the LGN differ primarily in their sensitivity to what?
options: Color and contrast vs. motion and luminance
questions.explanation: Magnocellular neurons are fast, low-acuity, motion/luminance tuned; parvocellular neurons carry high-acuity color/opponent signals; koniocellular neurons contribute blue/yellow and other modulatory signals.

questions.stem: Find the primary visual cortex, located in and around the calcarine sulcus.
questions.explanation: V1 (BA 17) lines the calcarine sulcus on the medial occipital surface; it receives the optic radiation from the LGN.

questions.stem: Find the thalamic relay that carries retinal signals to visual cortex.
questions.explanation: The lateral geniculate nucleus is the principal thalamic relay from retina to V1; the medial geniculate body instead serves the auditory system.
